title: Gap: rolling deploys corrupt stateful EFS when 2 tasks mount it concurrently
description: Default aws_ecs_service deployment_configuration = min 100% / max 200% means ECS starts a replacement task BEFORE stopping the old one on forceNewDeployment. For a service with a writable EFS volume (postgres being the canonical case), both tasks mount the same data dir for ~seconds; the new task's initdb wipes postgres's live data and both crash. Observed in Mini v3 smoke: Task A initialized, 'rc secrets push' triggered forceNewDeployment, Task B's initdb removed contents, Task A panicked, subsequent restarts found partial state and refused. Fix: when a service has ANY EFS volume mount, emit 'deployment_minimum_healthy_percent=0' and 'deployment_maximum_percent=100' so ECS stops the old task before starting the new one. Rolling remains the default for stateless services.

==============================================================

    - k8s (if kind + docker available)

  Runs: every commit

title: Phase 2: System requirements — Provider interface, rc.yml v2 schema, terraform backend
description: Translate Phase 1 requirements into concrete system-level contracts: (a) the Provider interface that ECS/k8s/future providers implement, (b) the rc.yml v2 schema (breaking change — tool ships rc migrate), (c) the terraform backend strategy (local vs S3 vs GCS — per-project choice), (d) the module directory layout that ensures cloud SDKs stay optional extras, (e) the migration path for the existing imperative services.
acceptance_criteria: Provider interface is defined with method signatures and contract semantics. rc.yml v2 schema is written out with every field documented. Terraform backend selection is specified. Directory layout decision is recorded. Migration plan from existing imperative services is captured.
notes:
PHASE 2 SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS

==============================================================
1. PROVIDER INTERFACE CONTRACT (Python ABC)
==============================================================

Module: remote_compose/provider/base.py

class Provider(ABC):
    name: str                                    # identifier ("ecs", "k8s", "fake")

    @abstractmethod
    def emit_terraform(self, ctx, out_dir) -> Path
        """FR-7: write standalone terraform module. Does not apply."""

    @abstractmethod
    def plan(self, ctx) -> PlanResult
        """terraform plan + structured diff"""

    @abstractmethod
    def deploy(self, ctx) -> DeployResult
        """idempotent apply: emit tf → terraform apply → build/push images → update services"""

    @abstractmethod
    def redeploy(self, ctx, services=None) -> DeployResult
        """force new revision without config change"""

    @abstractmethod
    def status(self, ctx) -> StatusReport

    @abstractmethod
    def logs(self, ctx, service, follow=False, tail=100) -> Iterator[str]

    @abstractmethod
    def exec(self, ctx, service, command, interactive=False) -> ExecResult

    @abstractmethod
    def rollback(self, ctx, to_revision=None) -> DeployResult

    @abstractmethod
    def destroy(self, ctx) -> None

Supporting dataclasses (remote_compose/provider/base.py):
  DeployContext  — project, compose, rc_yml_v2, provider_config, tf_backend_config, working_dir
  ServiceStatus  — name, desired, running, health, last_event
  DeployResult   — revision_id, services, duration, warnings, terraform_outputs
  PlanResult     — create/update/destroy counts, raw plan text
  StatusReport   — list[ServiceStatus], cluster_health, ingress_url
  ExecResult     — exit_code, stdout, stderr

Contract semantics (enforced by shared contract test suite):
  - All methods idempotent
  - State lives in terraform backend; Provider methods are stateless between invocations
  - emit_terraform output must be apply-able without the Provider (FR-7 gate)
  - build/push images is a separate ImageBuilder concern invoked by deploy()
  - Each method returns within a bounded time or raises ProviderTimeoutError

==============================================================
2. rc.yml v2 SCHEMA
==============================================================

      min: 1

    namespace: <ns>

    bucket: <name>

    region: us-west-2

    cpu: 1024
    memory: 4096
    replicas: 2

    launch_type: FARGATE              # optional override (ECS only)
    health_check_path: /api/health/

  region                 → provider_config.ecs.region
  aws_profile            → provider_config.ecs.aws_profile
  compose_file           → compose_file (unchanged)
  project_name           → project

==============================================================
3. TERRAFORM BACKEND STRATEGY
==============================================================

- User selects backend in rc.yml terraform.backend
- rc emits a backend.tf block with the chosen config; does not wrap or reimplement
- State reads go through `terraform output -json` (NFR-6 stateless CLI)
- Locking is backend-native (DynamoDB for s3, GCS object lock, etc.)
- Supported day 1: s3, local. Day 2: gcs, azurerm, remote.
- rc validates backend block but never reads raw state

title: Phase 1: Functional + non-functional requirements
description: Capture the full requirements set for the portable deployer as the first TDD gate. Covers inputs (standard docker-compose.yml + optional rc.yml v2), operations (deploy, redeploy, logs, exec, status, rollback, destroy), supported cloud features (secrets, persistent volumes, public ingress, service-to-service networking), and non-functional constraints (testable without cloud creds, idempotent, cloud SDKs as optional extras, compose as sole required input).
acceptance_criteria: Requirements list is complete enough that Phase 2 (system reqs) can start without ambiguity. Each requirement is individually testable or labelled non-testable with justification.
notes:
FINAL REQUIREMENTS — Phase 1

## Functional Requirements

FR-1 Input
- Accept any valid docker-compose.yml (v3+) unmodified as primary input
- Optional rc.yml v2 for deploy-time tuning
- Compose file is authoritative for services, images, ports, volumes, depends_on, env

FR-2 CLI Operations
- rc deploy — idempotent apply
- rc redeploy — force rollout without config change
- rc plan — preview (terraform plan)
- rc status — per-service state table
- rc logs <svc> — stream/tail container logs
- rc exec <svc> <cmd> — run command in live container
- rc rollback — revert to previous applied terraform state
- rc destroy — full teardown of what we created
- rc migrate — rc.yml v1 → v2

FR-3 Providers (v1)
- AWS ECS — both Fargate and EC2 launch types
- Kubernetes — any kubeconfig-reachable cluster; kind for local/CI
- Adding a third provider = implement Provider interface + ship terraform templates; no core changes

FR-3a ECS/EC2 specifics
- Managed capacity provider backed by Auto Scaling Group (Launch Template, instance type, min/max/desired)
- Task definitions emit correct requiresCompatibilities per launch type
- awsvpc as default network mode (required for Service Connect); bridge/host as escape hatches
- Mixed mode allowed: some services Fargate, some EC2, same cluster
- EFS volumes for persistence (works on both launch types)
- Fargate is default launch type; EC2 opt-in per service via rc.yml
- Instance type in rc.yml is optional — if absent, rc auto-sizes from summed service CPU/memory
- Both Spot and On-Demand supported for EC2 capacity; user-selectable in rc.yml

FR-4 Cloud feature parity across providers
- Secrets: env-var injection sourced from provider secret store (AWS Secrets Manager / k8s Secrets / ExternalSecrets)
- Persistent volumes: compose named volumes → provider-native persistent storage (EFS / PVC)
- Public ingress: at least one HTTP service exposed via provider LB (ALB / Ingress)
- Service-to-service networking: by compose service name (Service Connect / k8s DNS)
- Health checks: per-service health endpoint drives provider readiness/liveness

FR-5 Image build & push
- Build from compose build: contexts
- Push to provider-appropriate registry (ECR / GCR / any OCI)
- Support pre-built image references (skip build)

FR-6 rc.yml v2 surface
- provider — which provider to use
- provider_config — provider-specific tuning (region, cluster, launch type, capacity, etc.)
- Per-service: resources (cpu/mem/replicas), type hint (app/worker/infra/proxy), health path, public/port, launch_type override (ECS)
- secrets — references, not values
- backup — S3/GCS bucket for DB dumps
- domain / tls — public hostname config

FR-7 Terraform portability (first-class)
- Emitted terraform module is self-contained and runnable standalone (terraform init && terraform apply) without rc installed
- Output at user-visible path (default ./terraform/<provider>/, configurable), not hidden under .rc/
- Follows HashiCorp conventions: main.tf / variables.tf / outputs.tf / auto-generated README.md
- Version-controllable: users can commit the generated module and manage infra with vanilla terraform thereafter
- rc never requires state or metadata that is not inside the terraform module itself

## Non-Functional Requirements

NFR-1 Testable without cloud — ≥80% of test suite runs with zero cloud creds (FakeProvider + moto + kind)
NFR-2 Idempotent — re-running deploy with unchanged config is a no-op; partial failures reconcile, not duplicate
NFR-3 Optional cloud SDKs — core has no boto3/kubernetes/google-cloud deps; providers ship as extras (pip install remote-compose[ecs], [k8s])
NFR-4 Compose-first — rc.yml optional; sensible defaults if absent
NFR-5 Observable — step-by-step progress, actionable errors; preserve current 15-step UX quality
NFR-6 Stateless CLI — terraform backend owns state; any machine with creds + backend access can operate; rc is a generator + convenience wrapper, not a lock-in
NFR-7 Reversible — destroy fully removes what deploy created; rollback uses terraform state history
NFR-8 Performance — code-only redeploy on equivalent stack completes in ≤2× current 630s

## Non-Goals

NG-1 Not a general orchestrator — no custom helm/kustomize/argo; use them via terraform when useful
NG-2 Not a CI/CD tool — rc deploy is the action; CI wiring is user's problem
NG-3 Not a secrets manager — we reference provider secrets, don't store or rotate
NG-4 No proprietary compose extensions — no x-rc-* keys in compose; tuning lives in rc.yml
NG-5 No live cross-provider migration — moving ECS→k8s is destroy+deploy with user-driven data migration

## Locked decisions

- Launch type default: Fargate, EC2 opt-in per service
- Instance type for EC2: user-specified in rc.yml, else auto-sized from summed CPU/memory
- Spot + On-Demand: both supported, user-selectable
- rc.yml: breaking v2 schema with rc migrate tool for v1→v2
- Terraform backend: user chooses (local/S3/GCS/etc.) — rc does not reinvent state
close_reason: Requirements locked: FR-1 through FR-7, NFR-1 through NFR-8, NG-1 through NG-5. Launch type, instance sizing, and Spot/On-Demand decisions recorded.

title: Ergonomics: ECS execute-command silently swallows script stdout from non-TTY
description: aws ecs execute-command invoked with 'tail -f /dev/null | ...' (required to keep stdin open from Claude Code Bash tool) reliably swallows stdout from non-trivial scripts. Simple commands like 'curl | tail' work, but base64-decoded scripts with pipes, heredocs, or stdout-to-file show an empty output file even when the script clearly ran to completion (verified by side effects). Affects debugging and any validation that relies on stdout. Workarounds tried: redirect inside container to /tmp/x.log then cat; still empty. Root cause likely in the SSM agent's handling of stdout when the local client disconnects too fast after the shell exits. Investigate: (a) explicit flush/sleep at script end, (b) write results to S3 via presigned URL and fetch locally, (c) have rc exec open a proper pty via script/expect.

title: Phase 6b.15: EFS encryption broken on accounts without alias/aws/elasticfilesystem
description: Cloud smoke error: 'The specified KMS key could not be found.' AWS returns this when creating an encrypted EFS in an account that has never used EFS — the aws-managed alias/aws/elasticfilesystem key doesn't auto-create via API (only via console). Fix: default encrypted=false with a prominent comment that production users should set encrypted=true + specify kms_key_id. OR: have the provider create the alias via aws_kms_alias + aws_kms_key before the EFS. For now default to unencrypted since this is infrastructure a user inherits; compliance can override.
acceptance_criteria: Fresh account with no pre-existing EFS resources can run rc deploy and EFS creation succeeds without manual KMS setup.

title: Phase 6b.14: EC2 launch type needs NAT gateway OR public subnet placement
description: Cloud smoke against real AWS caught this: aws_autoscaling_group launches EC2 instances into private subnets (aws_subnet.private[*].id) but there's no NAT gateway. Instances have no internet path to pull the ECS agent, ECR images, or register with the cluster. ASG waits 10 min then times out. Options: (a) add NAT gateway (production-correct, ~$0.045/hr, needs reap support); (b) default to public subnets with associate_public_ip_address=true on the launch template network_interfaces block (simpler, cheaper, slightly less secure); (c) use VPC endpoints for ECS + ECR + S3 + CloudWatch (no NAT needed but more HCL). Recommend (b) as default with (a)/(c) opt-in via rc.yml.
acceptance_criteria: A fresh rc deploy with launch_type=EC2 brings the ASG instance healthy within 3 minutes and the worker service starts tasks. Reap script cleans up NAT gateway (if used) and all EC2 network artifacts.
notes: Expanded scope: NOT just EC2. Also Fargate tasks need internet path to pull ECR images (same root cause — no NAT in private subnets). Current fix: Fargate tasks placed in PUBLIC subnets with assign_public_ip=true + tasks SG restricting inbound to ALB SG + self. Cost savings: ~$0.045/hr skipped NAT. Security: SG lockdown means public IP is egress-only. Future: opt-in private-subnet-with-NAT for users who need it.

Work: (a) parse compose build: stanzas during DeployContext construction; (b) in provider.deploy, after apply, for each service with a build context: authenticate to ECR (boto3 ecr.get_authorization_token), tag image with ECR URL + a content hash tag, ImageBuilder.build, ImagePusher.push; (c) update task def to reference the specific tag (not :latest) OR force-new-deployment to pull latest; (d) emit structured progress like the legacy 15-step pipeline.
acceptance_criteria: From examples/demo-app with docker running + AWS creds,  builds and pushes the api + worker images to fresh ECR repos, ECS services start successfully, ALB returns 200 on /health. Subsequent rc deploy with unchanged code is a no-op (idempotent image tag based on source hash).

title: Stale terraform 1.1.7 install causes subprocess SIGKILL (not sandbox)
description: Originally misdiagnosed as a Claude Code sandbox issue. Reality: the Homebrew terraform formula on the dev Mac is 1.1.7 from 2022-03 (4+ years stale, x86_64 on macOS 15 with modern Gatekeeper) and macOS kills the subprocess on exec. Reproduces identically outside any sandbox — this was never a sandbox bug. Proper fix: rc doctor / rc install upgrades terraform via brew; template requires terraform >= 1.5 anyway. Flagged beads, ARCHITECTURE.md sandbox claims, and integration-test sentinel comments all need the 'sandbox' wording rewritten.
notes: Root cause: stale brew install + Gatekeeper kill on macOS. Symptoms: subprocess exit codes -9 / 137. Diagnosis trail: sysctl confirmed Intel Mac (not Apple Silicon / Rosetta), terraform binary linked to Cellar/terraform/1.1.7, user confirmed it's an old Intel box. Action: rc-e5u.21 (rc doctor) handles this generically. In-session work that I claimed was 'blocked by sandbox' can actually run on this box once terraform is upgraded.
close_reason: Resolved by rc-e5u.21 (rc doctor / rc install). The root cause was stale brew install, not a sandbox — rc doctor --fix now upgrades terraform via the platform package manager. Not a live issue.

title: Phase 5: Architecture — module layout, deprecation plan for imperative services
description: Lock the module layout before implementation starts. Decide where the Provider interface lives, where each provider's code + terraform templates live, how rc.yml v2 parsing/migration is organized, how the CLI dispatches to providers, and how the existing imperative services (aws_service, ecs_service, efs_service, etc.) are deprecated incrementally rather than deleted. Also settle how terraform is invoked (subprocess vs python-terraform library) and how terraform state is passed to the CLI for status/logs queries.
acceptance_criteria: Module tree is drawn with file paths. Each existing imperative service has a planned fate (keep, replace, delete, wrap). Terraform invocation approach is chosen. CLI dispatch mechanism is specified.
notes:
PHASE 5 ARCHITECTURE

Module layout, import rules, and imperative-service deprecation plan are fully
specified in the Phase 2 notes (rc-e5u.2). This phase adds the three
architectural pieces not covered there:

==============================================================
1. CLI DISPATCH MECHANISM
==============================================================

- Existing cli.py (Click-based) stays as the entry point; no rewrite.
- Each top-level command (deploy / plan / status / logs / exec / rollback /
  destroy / redeploy / migrate) resolves a Provider instance once:
      provider = remote_compose.provider.get(rc_yml.provider)()
  Then delegates:
      provider.deploy(ctx)  # or plan/status/... depending on command
- --provider <name> flag overrides rc.yml for one-off testing.
- Provider is resolved via the registry populated at import time by
  remote_compose.provider.{fake,ecs,k8s}.
- Every provider module self-registers: its __init__ calls
  remote_compose.provider.register(name, cls).

==============================================================
2. ERROR HANDLING
==============================================================

- All provider-surfaced exceptions derive from ProviderError
  (see remote_compose/provider/base.py).
- CLI top-level catches ProviderError, prints the sanitized message to stderr,
  exits non-zero. Existing log_sanitizer is reused.
- --verbose flag promotes to traceback printing.
- Unexpected (non-ProviderError) exceptions always print traceback — those
  are bugs, not user errors.

==============================================================
3. PROGRESS REPORTING  (NFR-5)
==============================================================

- Current 15-step pipeline output (`[N/M] StepName... done (Xs)`) is the UX
  baseline.
- Introduce a ProgressReporter protocol:
      class ProgressReporter(Protocol):
          def step(self, idx: int, total: int, name: str) -> "StepCtx": ...
          class StepCtx:
              def done(self, duration_s: float, warnings: list[str]): ...
              def fail(self, err: Exception): ...
- Providers accept a ProgressReporter in their constructor (default =
  TtyProgressReporter). Tests inject a RecordingProgressReporter to assert
  on the step sequence without touching stdout.
- This replaces the deployment_pipeline step abstraction but preserves its
  user-visible output.

==============================================================
REMAINING ARCHITECTURAL ITEMS — DEFERRED
==============================================================

- Concurrency model for Provider.deploy (ServiceSpec parallelism). Default
  sequential at first; revisit when a real deployment motivates it.
- Pluggable terraform-runner backends (subprocess vs library). Locked to
  subprocess per Phase 2; no change here.
- Output format for machine-readable CLI (--json). Nice to have, not in v1
  scope.

value: Mini v0 runbook (ss migration us-west-1 smoke): 1) rc.yml tailored with project=rc-test-*, region=us-west-1, vpc_cidr=10.42.0.0/16, aws_profile=debuggai. 2) Stub docker-compose.yml with public images (busybox:latest for app/workers, postgres:16-alpine, redis:7-alpine, nginx:alpine). 3) For Mini v0 specifically: skip postgres volumes (hits rc-e5u.27 EFS chown bug) and set nginx health_check_path: / (stock nginx:alpine 404s on /health). 4) rc deploy fresh ~200s, redeploy ~70s. 5) Post-destroy verify needs manual cleanup of /aws/ecs/containerinsights/<cluster>/performance log group (provider gap, filed). 6) Verification sweep: ecs clusters, VPCs tagged Project, ALBs, target groups, EFS, ECR, servicediscovery namespaces, log groups, IAM roles starting rc-test-, secrets, security groups by tag.

Mini v2 secrets workflow (v2 rc.yml + per-key SM): (1) declare secrets with source=file+path in rc.yml; (2) rc deploy creates SM placeholders + task defs referencing arn:KEY:: per key; (3) tasks will fail health until secrets are real — this is expected; (4) rc secrets push parses each .env file, puts SecretString=json.dumps({KEY:value}), force-rolls services; (5) tasks boot with env vars from SM. Caveat: django entrypoint does NOT run migrations — 'aws ecs execute-command django -- python manage.py migrate --noinput' is a required post-secrets step, else admin hits 'relation django_site does not exist'. createsuperuser --noinput honors DJANGO_SUPERUSER_{EMAIL,PASSWORD} when USERNAME_FIELD='email' on User model. Every task def currently gets ALL secrets across ALL services — tracked as follow-up bead for per-service scoping.

start-simpli admin login requires EMAIL in the 'Email address' form field (USERNAME_FIELD='email' in apps/users/models.py). Django createsuperuser --noinput honors DJANGO_SUPERUSER_EMAIL + _PASSWORD; the _USERNAME env is ignored when USERNAME_FIELD is not 'username'. Custom csrf_failure handler at apps/authentication/views.csrf_failure returns JSON {error:CSRF_VALIDATION_FAILED}, easy to mistake for a real CSRF issue vs stale cookies. ALB target group gets new DNS name on each cold stack (e.g. alb-1509417821) so CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS env must be updated + redeployed after first deploy, or use ALLOWED_HOSTS='*' + skip CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS for test stacks.

Mini v3 stateful EFS runbook: (1) rc.yml volumes entry gains optional uid/gid/mode (default 1000/1000/0755). postgres:16-alpine = 70, postgres (debian) = 999, redis:7-alpine = 999, mysql = 999. Mode 0700 for db dirs. (2) Provider auto-sets deployment_minimum_healthy_percent=0/maximum=100 on ANY service with EFS mounts — rolling deploys corrupt stateful EFS when two tasks briefly mount the same dir. (3) postgres-on-EFS baseline throughput is slow: 50KB/s per GiB stored, ~100 MiB/s burst initially. Big restores can take hours. (4) aws ecs execute-command swallows stdout from complex scripts in non-TTY mode — base64+heredoc+pipe scripts run correctly but return empty output. Use side-effect tests (curl ALB) for reality-check.
